newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia may revise budget dividend ruling - source.
newsitem.headline: Australia may revise budget dividend ruling - source.

text.p: A determined campaign by Australian fund managers and market officials has forced the government to consider winding back controversial changes to dividend taxation rules announced in the May budget.
Industry and government sources told Reuters the Australian Taxation Office and Treasury Department were redrafting some key elements following two days of meetings in Canberra this week.
One government source said the new proposals were likely to be sent to Treasurer Peter Costello within two weeks and would recognise that the original set of rules was excessive.

The surprise restrictions on both franking credits and the use of hedging instruments had led the funds management industry to publicly warn that derivatives markets and Australia's wider reputation as a capital-raising centre were now under threat.
"I think the Treasury and Tax Office realise now that attacking hedging goes beyond their real brief which is to cut out franking trading," said one source.
The government said in its May 13 budget that it planned to stop a market technique used by some savvy local brokers and investors called "dividend washing".

Under this scheme, a foreign company sells stock near the dividend payment date and repurchases it once a local investor has absorbed the franking credits. Australia's tax system recognises that once a company has paid tax it should not be paid again by investors who receive dividends from the firm.
Apart from fund managers, the latest meeting was attended by officials from the Australian Stock Exchange and the Sydney Futures exchange, as well as private sector tax advisers.
The departments received 30 critical submissions following the first meeting with industry groups held in late May.

One source who attended the meeting said that as far as superannuation funds were concerned, the government was now likely to scrap the "no trade" rule where franking credits would be denied to investors if they bought or sold shares within 45 days. The industry hoped this revision would be applied to other investors but there were no guarantees given at the meeting.
The source also said the government was expected to overturn the budget ruling that removed franking credits for investors who hedged 70 percent or more of their portfolio.
Under the revised proposal, the credits would remain available to investors who hedged on the downside only.
Another industry source said the government did not plan any more meetings with the industry so the exact nature of the changes would not be known until the treasurer issued a statement.
"They (the government) are giving veiled messages so that people are feeling reasonably comfortable that they will end up paring back their proposals a fair bit," said the source.
"But none of us can feel absolutely confident how they are yet planning to do it."
